posts.post_subject: It'll take some smarts to make this holography idea work
posts.content_md:
8) Before the next phase of space exploration they should test it in the holography lab.

What if we take the glass plane a 3-D image can be projected on and cut it into millions of pieces and throw them up like confetti? Not practical.

O.K. Let's take the [smart dust](http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/6566317.stm) that scientists plan to use to explore other planets, strip off the sensors and use a foil-like layer over the microchip. The smart dust's layer could still be contorted by voltage so it will hover aerodynamically. Aim a laser system at the swarm of floating reflectors and we'd truly have a floating hologram you could walk into (just don't breathe in).

> **DrOutlier:** 8) O.K. Let's take the smart dust that scientists plan to use to explore other planets, strip off the sensors and use a foil-like layer over the microchip. The smart dust's layer could still be contorted by voltage so it will hover aerodynamically. Aim a laser system at the swarm of floating reflectors and we'd truly have a floating hologram you could walk into (just don't breathe in).

May be it can be done without laser system at all. If every smart dust particle contains a tiny GPS sensor, an indexed memory and a multi-color

LED, we can program them individually so they will know which color to shine for every 3d coordinate. Simply let them fly chaotically, and they will show a 3d picture.

Saludos,

Raúl.

posts.post_subject: It'll take some smarts to make this holography idea work
posts.content_md:
8) Both are great suggestions I hadn't considered. Brilliant suggestion stereofan! I like the LEDs idea also but since they need voltage (tiny) to stay up I don't know if the power supply could handle the load of a bright enough LED. Maybe it would if the sensors we would strip off are an equal enough load. Or we just use more smart dust for brightness. Darn it! Now you made me think of The Outer Limits episode, "Small Friends". 

Also, the GPS is a pracical problem outside of DARPA. For some reason GPS with millimeter accuracy is seen as more of a security risk than the present accuracy. We'll have it soon enough I am sure. The shortest kept secret is military technology and the advantages of nanotechnology in the next decade will outpace the perceived risk.

Hi -

You might be entertained to hear that Jeff Han (of CU-SeeMe and the multi-touch table) started working on a volumetric 3-D display that will attempt to ascertain where dust particles are in the air, and then illuminate them at just the right time. He calls it ["Holodust."](http://cs.nyu.edu/~jhan/holodust/index.html)

I agree that orientation-aware well-distributed light sources can make 3-D imagery. We did some thought in this area several years back. (Does this [image link](http://aiw1.uspto.gov:80/.aiw?Docid=20030146908&homeurl=http%3A%2F%2Fappft1.uspto.gov%2Fnetacgi%2Fnph-Parser%3FSect1%3DPTO1%2526Sect2%3DHITOFF%2526d%3DPG01%2526p%3D1%2526u%3D%25252Fnetahtml%25252FPTO%25252Fsrchnum.html%2526r%3D1%2526f%3DG%2526l%3D50%2526s1%3D%25252220030146908%252522.PGNR.%2526OS%3DDN%2F20030146908%2526RS%3DDN%2F20030146908&PageNum=&Rtype=&SectionNum=&idkey=D2C1219DF9B9) work?)
